moneymaker-farha-2003/after-turn.text: Moneymaker doesn't just call. He raises, with a hand that hasn't actually made anything yet. Farha calls.

moneymaker-farha-2003/flop.text: Nine, deuce, six. Two spades out there. The hole-card camera tells us Farha has a pair of nines. You have king high and one spade toward a flush. He checks. So do you.

moneymaker-farha-2003/open.text: Two thousand three. The final table of the World Series of Poker. On one side, Sammy Farha, a professional, cigarette hanging off his lip. On the other, Chris Moneymaker, an accountant from Nashville who bought into this thing for forty dollars online. You're in Moneymaker's seat.

moneymaker-farha-2003/preflop.text: You look down at a king and a seven. Nothing special. You raise anyway, just to see what the flop brings.

moneymaker-farha-2003/river.text: Three of hearts. A blank. No spade, no straight. You have king high, which beats nothing at all. And Farha checks, still holding his pair of nines.

moneymaker-farha-2003/river-context.text: So here it is. Nearly two million in the middle, and the only way to win it is to make a professional fold a made hand for his tournament life.

moneymaker-farha-2003/turn.text: There's your third spade. Now you've got a real draw. One more spade makes a flush, and any five or any ten makes you a straight.

moneymaker-farha-2003/turn-bet.text: And Farha fires out more than the size of the pot. He's protecting those nines. This one's yours.
